L13: # Data Independence
L14: A program P is data independent with respect to a data type X iff it does not use any operations and predicates involving values of type X other than equality tests. It is also allowed to input, output and nondeterministically choose values of type X, as well as store them and copy them within its variables. When P is data independent with respect to X, it is parameterised by X. In other words, any concrete data type can be instantiated for X in P.
L15: Given a specification S and a program P which are data independent with respect to a data type X, our main results on data independence enable the problem of verifying whether S is satisfied by P for all instances of X to be reduced to verifying the satisfaction for a finite number of finite instances. The body of research by which such results are proved is a semantic study of data independence consisting of symbolic operational semantics, logical relations, and symmetry elimination.
L16: Most of our research on data independence so far has been in terms of the CSP formalism. The basic part of the work can be found in Section 15.2 of "The Theory and Practice" book by A. W. Roscoe (available electronically in our 【11†books†web.comlab.ox.ac.uk】 section) and, in more detail, in Lazic's 【12†thesis†web.comlab.ox.ac.uk】.
L17: There also are papers on the extension by arrays in the context of determinism checking, and on the extension by generalised predicate symbols (see the group's 【13†publications page†web.comlab.ox.ac.uk】).

L33: ## Radu Grigore ; Nikos Tzevelekos - History-Register Automata
L34: 
L35: lmcs:1630 - Logical Methods in Computer Science, March 29, 2016, Volume 12, Issue 1 - 【30†https://doi.org/10.2168/LMCS-12(1:7)2016†doi.org】
L36: 
L37: History-Register Automata Article
L38: 
L39: Authors: Radu Grigore ; Nikos Tzevelekos
L40: Programs with dynamic allocation are able to create and use an unbounded number of fresh resources, such as references, objects, files, etc. We propose History-Register Automata (HRA), a new automata-theoretic formalism for modelling such programs. HRAs extend the expressiveness of previous approaches and bring us to the limits of decidability for reachability checks.
L41: The distinctive feature of our machines is their use of unbounded memory sets (histories) where input symbols can be selectively stored and compared with symbols to follow. In addition, stored symbols can be consumed or deleted by reset. We show that the combination of consumption and reset capabilities renders the automata powerful enough to imitate counter machines, and yields closure under all regular operations apart from complementation.
L42: We moreover examine weaker notions of HRAs which strike different balances between expressiveness and effectiveness.

L151: ## Abstract
L152:     We introduce a Hennessy-Milner logic with recursion for Fresh Labelled Transition Systems (FLTSs). These are nominal labelled transition systems which keep track of the history, i.e. of data values seen so far, and can model fresh data generation. In particular, FLTSs generalise the computations of Fresh-Register Automata, which in turn can be seen as a "regular" class of history-tracking automata operating on infinite input alphabets.
L153: The logic we introduce is a modal mu-calculus equipped with infinite disjunctions over arbitrary and fresh data values respectively, while its recursion is parameterised on vectors of data values. It can express a variety of properties, such as the existence of an infinite path of distinct data values, the absence of paths where values are repeated, or the existence of a finite path where some taint property is violated.
L154: We study the model-checking problem and its complexity via a reduction to parity games and, using nominal sets techniques, provide an exponential upper bound for it.

L30: # Register Automaton with Fresh Value Generation
L31: 
L32: Existing register automaton models do not allow for the generation of fresh output values. This feature is technically challenging due to the resulting non-determinism. Fresh outputs, however, are crucial in many real-world systems, e.g. servers that generate fresh identifiers, passwords or sequence numbers. That's why we extended the register automaton model with Fresh Value generation.
L33: ## Formal definition Register Automaton with Fresh Value Generation
L34: 
L35: Source: [【17†TomteFreshJournal】]
L36: 
L37: In this section, we define register automata. For reasons of exposition, the notion of register automaton that we define here is a simplified version which can be easily be extended with constants and actions with multiple parameters.
L38: We postulate a countably infinite set V of variables which contains two special variables `in` and `out` which are used to specify the data parameter of input and output actions, respectively. An atomic formula is a boolean expression of the form true, false, x=y or x≠y, with x,y∈V. A formula φ is a conjunction of atomic formulas. Let X⊆V be a set of variables. We write Φ(X) for the set of formulas with variables taken from X. A valuation for X is a function ξ:X→Z.
L39: We write Val(X) for the set of valuations for X.
L40: Thus:
L41: 
L42: V
L43:     a countably infinite set of variables
L44: Φ(X)
L45:     the set of formulas with variables taken from X, where a formula is a conjunction of atomic formulas of the form true, false, x=y or x≠y, with x,y∈X.
L46: 
L47: Definition 1 (Register automaton). A register automaton (RA) is a tuple R=(I,O,L,l_{0},R,Γ) with
L48:   * I and O finite, disjoint sets of input and output symbols, respectively,
L49:   * L a finite set of locations and l_{0} ∈ L the initial location,
L50:   * R is a function that assigns to each location l a finite set R(l)⊆V\{`in`,`out`} of registers, with R(l_{0})=∅
L51:   * Γ ⊆ L × I × Φ(V) × (V ↛ V) × O × L a finite set of transitions.
L52:   * In a transition (l,i,G,U,o,l′)∈Γ, we refer to
L53:     * l as the source location,
L54:     * i as the input symbol,
L55:     * G as the guard function,
L56:     * U as the update function (a partial function),
L57:     * o as the output symbol, and
L58:     * l′ as the target location.
L59:   * For each transition (l,i,G,U,o,l′)∈Γ, we require that:
L60:     * G∈Φ( R(l)∪{in,out} ) and
L61:     * U:R(l′)→R(l)∪{in,out}.
L62: The operational semantics of a register automaton is a Mealy machine in which the states are pairs of a location l and a valuation ξ of the registers R(l). A transition may fire for given input and output values if its guard evaluates to true. In this case, a new valuation of the registers R(l′) is computed using the update part of the transition.
L63: 
L64: For the formal definition of the operational semantics of register automata in terms of Mealy machines we refer to [【17†TomteFreshJournal】].
L65: ## Example
L66: 
L67: As a first running example of a register automaton we use a FIFO-set with capacity two. A FIFO-set is a queue in which only different values can be stored, see Figure 1.
L68: 
L69: Fig. 1.FIFO-set with a capacity of 2 modeled as a register automatonThe operational semantics of register automata is defined in terms of (infinite state) Mealy machines.
L70: Input `Push` tries to insert a value in the queue, and input `Pop` tries to retrieve a value from the queue. The output in response to a `Push` is `OK` if the input value can be added successfully, or `NOK` if the input value is already in the queue or if the queue is full. The output in response to a `Pop` is `Return`, with as parameter the oldest value from the queue, or `NOK` if the queue is empty.
L71: We omit parameters that do not matter, and for instance write `Pop()` instead of `Pop(in)` if parameter 𝗂𝗇 does not occur in the guard and is not touched by the update.
